Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Vignette:
Arthur, at sixty-nine, had built a life on the principles of order and predictability. As a financial analyst, he managed risk by understanding patterns and projecting outcomes, a skill that had always provided a sense of control. For the past eighteen months, however, since the morning his wife Eleanor died, that control had been an illusion. The trauma was not an event he could analyze; it was a permanent feature of his internal landscape. It had happened on a Tuesday. He was in the kitchen making tea when he heard the teacup shatter in the living room. He found Eleanor on the floor, her eyes wide with a terror he had never seen, one hand clutching her chest. The minutes that followed were a chaotic blur of him fumbling with his phone to call 911, the dispatcher’s calm voice a bizarre counterpoint to his own frantic heartbeat, and the suffocating helplessness of watching the life drain from the person he had known for forty-five years.

Now, that memory is an ambush. It can strike anywhere, without warning. A few weeks ago, while reviewing quarterly earnings reports in the quiet of his office, the image of Eleanor’s face flashed behind his eyes. It was not a gentle recollection but a full-sensory replay. He could feel the cold sweat on his own brow, his heart began to pound against his ribs with the same frantic rhythm as it had that morning, and he had to grip his desk to keep from crying out. He has come to believe these feelings—the horror, the guilt, the raw, serrated edge of grief—are dangerous. He is certain that if he allows them to take hold, they will consume him entirely, a tidal wave from which he will never surface. His life has since become a complex, exhausting exercise in prevention.

Anything that might remind him of Eleanor, or of loss in general, is now a threat to be managed. He began by trying to simply push the thoughts away, a constant, draining mental effort to redirect his focus to anything else—market trends, stock valuations, the meticulous details of his work. When that wasn't enough, he began dismantling the life they had built. He avoids the Italian restaurant they loved, the park where they used to walk, and has stopped returning calls from their mutual friends. He feels a pang of guilt, but the fear of a casual "I remember when you and Eleanor..." is far stronger. This avoidance extends beyond his own loss. When a junior analyst at his firm recently lost his father, Arthur found himself unable to offer condolences. The mere mention of a funeral sent a jolt of panic through him, and he spent the rest of the day locked in his office, pretending to be on a conference call.

This constant vigilance has left him brittle. His colleagues, who once saw him as a steady, if quiet, mentor, now tread carefully around him. The other day, a younger team member was sharing a story about his grandmother passing away, and Arthur, feeling the familiar surge of panic and a hot flush of anger, snapped at him to “keep personal matters out of the office.” The young man’s shocked silence was a mirror of Arthur’s own shame, but the outburst had served its purpose: it stopped the conversation. He numbs the feelings that still manage to break through his defenses, often with a glass of scotch—then a second—the moment he gets home, the warmth in his chest a dull substitute for any real emotion. He no longer feels joy or affection, only a gray, hollowed-out exhaustion and the simmering irritation that lies beneath it. It was after his daughter called, crying, to ask why he had refused to visit his wife’s grave on her birthday, that Arthur finally conceded something was deeply wrong. He is terrified of feeling the full weight of his grief, but he has realized, with a chilling clarity, that the life he is living now—an empty fortress built to keep pain out—is hardly a life at all.
